title: RTOS & Real-Time Concepts
relevance: Tests whether candidates understand deadline-driven correctness, preemptive scheduling, and concurrency hazards that show up in embedded and systems SDE interviews.

phases.goal: Establish what real-time means and when a superloop fails versus an RTOS.

must_hit.point: A real-time system is correct only if the logically correct result is produced before a strict deadline, prioritizing determinism over raw throughput.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts a fast non-deadline computation (e.g. pi) with an engine controller that fails if injection timing is late.

must_hit.point: Hard real-time: missing a deadline is total system failure; firm: late result is useless but system survives; soft: missed deadlines degrade performance but are tolerated.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives matching examples such as flight control/airbags, dropped late video frames, and UI updates.

must_hit.point: A bare-metal superloop runs handlers sequentially in an infinite while(1); one slow call delays later critical work.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes cooperative sequential handlers and how a slow update_display delays control_motor.

must_hit.point: An RTOS adds preemptive multitasking so a high-priority task can interrupt a low-priority one to guarantee response times.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States you need an RTOS when timing dependencies between independent events are too complex for a linear loop.

probes: What makes a system real-time versus merely fast?
When does a bare-metal superloop stop being enough?

hints.1: Think about deadlines, not just speed.
hints.2: Compare sequential while(1) handlers with forced preemption by priority.
hints.3: Hard/firm/soft classify deadline misses; RTOS preempts low-priority work so high-priority work meets timing.

phases.goal: Explain tasks, states, the system tick, context switches, and RTOS IPC primitives.

must_hit.point: Each task is an infinite loop with its own private stack; the RTOS tracks its context as the CPU register state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says each task thinks it owns the CPU; illusion comes from per-task stack plus saved registers.

must_hit.point: A hardware timer fires a periodic system tick; at each tick or yield, the scheduler runs the highest-priority ready task.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions a periodic tick interrupt and priority-based selection of the next task.

must_hit.point: Task states include Running (one per core), Ready, Blocked (waiting for an event), and Suspended (explicitly paused).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines Ready as waiting because a higher or equal priority task is Running; Blocked as waiting for timer/message/lock.

must_hit.point: A context switch saves Task A's registers onto A's stack, swaps stack pointers, and restores Task B's registers—preemptive priority-based scheduling.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks push-save-SP / load-SP / pop for the switch between tasks.

must_hit.point: IPC primitives: mutex (owned token for shared resources), binary/counting semaphore (no owner; signaling/resource counts), message queues (thread-safe FIFO by copy), and event flags (bitmasks).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes mutex ownership from semaphore signaling and queue-by-copy vs shared memory.

must_hit.point: A blocked delay does not spin: the scheduler marks the task Blocked and will not schedule it until the delay elapses.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Corrects the myth that vTaskDelay-style waits burn CPU in a while loop.

probes: What happens on a context switch between two tasks?
How do mutexes, semaphores, and queues differ for inter-task communication?

hints.1: Start from one CPU core sharing time across tasks.
hints.2: Cover tick → scheduler → states → stack/context, then the four IPC tools.
hints.3: Running/Ready/Blocked/Suspended; switch saves/restores registers via each task's stack; mutex has ownership, semaphore does not.

phases.goal: Surface priority inversion, mutex vs semaphore, deadlock conditions, and real-time memory choices.

must_hit.point: Priority inversion: a high-priority task waits on a mutex held by a low-priority task that is then preempted by a medium-priority task, so the high task effectively runs at the low priority.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Tells the VIP/janitor/customer story or the Mars Pathfinder bus-mutex case.

must_hit.point: Priority inheritance elevates the low-priority mutex holder to the blocked high priority until it releases the mutex, then priority drops back.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains temporary elevation so medium tasks cannot preempt the holder.

must_hit.point: Prefer a mutex over a binary semaphore to protect shared resources because only ownership enables priority inheritance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States binary semaphores lack ownership so the RTOS cannot apply priority inheritance.

must_hit.point: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the four conditions and notes consistent lock ordering breaks circular wait.

must_hit.point: Dynamic malloc/free is discouraged: non-deterministic timing and heap fragmentation risk; high-reliability systems statically allocate stacks and queues at compile time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts variable-time heap use with compile-time static allocation of task stacks and queues.

probes: What is priority inversion and how does priority inheritance fix it?
Why protect a shared resource with a mutex rather than a binary semaphore?

hints.1: Picture high blocked on low while medium keeps running.
hints.2: Connect mutex ownership to inheritance; list Coffman for deadlock.
hints.3: Inheritance boosts the holder to high until unlock; no ownership ⇒ no inheritance; order locks consistently to break circular wait.

phases.goal: Apply deferred ISR work, schedulability ideas, and concrete producer/consumer and inheritance timelines.

must_hit.point: ISRs preempt everything and must stay short: clear the hardware flag, wake a task via semaphore/queue, never call standard blocking RTOS APIs from an interrupt.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes deferral to a high-priority handler task and FromISR-style APIs.

must_hit.point: Interrupt latency is time from hardware trigger to the ISR's first instruction; scheduling latency is time from the ISR making a task Ready until that task is Running.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines both latencies as the two measures of responsiveness.

must_hit.point: Rate-monotonic scheduling assigns highest priorities to shortest-period (most frequent) tasks; if total CPU utilization stays below roughly 69%, independent tasks are guaranteed to meet deadlines.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States Liu and Layland rule: highest priority to most frequent; cites the utilization bound from the file.

must_hit.point: Every task needs its own stack; undersizing causes stack overflow that can silently corrupt an adjacent task's memory (often the TCB).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links under-estimated stacks to bizarre crashes via overwrite of neighboring task state.

must_hit.point: In priority inheritance: Low takes mutex, High blocks and Low is raised to High's priority so Medium cannot preempt Low until the mutex is given back.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the Low/High/Medium timeline where elevated Low finishes before Medium runs.

probes: How should an ISR hand work to a task under an RTOS?
How does rate-monotonic scheduling assign priorities, and what utilization bound is cited for independent tasks?

hints.2: Name FromISR give/send, then RMS shortest-period-first and stack-per-task.
hints.3: Clear flag → xSemaphoreGiveFromISR/queue FromISR → handler task; RMS highest priority to shortest period; ~69% utilization bound for the guarantee.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: A superloop is simple cooperative sequencing but one slow handler delays critical work; an RTOS preempts by priority so independent timing dependencies can meet response guarantees when a linear loop cannot.

tradeoffs.topic: Mutex vs binary semaphore for shared resources
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A mutex has ownership so the RTOS can apply priority inheritance; a binary semaphore has no owner, so unbounded priority inversion cannot be prevented the same way.

tradeoffs.topic: Dynamic allocation vs static allocation in real-time systems
tradeoffs.strong_answer: malloc/free take variable time and risk fragmentation; statically allocating task stacks and queues at compile time keeps timing deterministic.

tradeoffs.topic: Process in ISR vs defer to a task
tradeoffs.strong_answer: ISRs preempt everything and must be short—clear the flag and signal a handler task; never call standard blocking RTOS functions inside an interrupt.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a blocked delay (e.g. vTaskDelay) spins in a while loop burning CPU.
gotchas.correction: The scheduler marks the task Blocked, swaps it out, and does not schedule it again until the delay elapses, so other tasks get the CPU.

gotchas.trap: Two tasks share the exact same highest priority and never block.
gotchas.correction: They typically time-slice round-robin every tick, wasting CPU on constant context switches.

gotchas.trap: Using a binary semaphore to protect a shared resource.
gotchas.correction: Without ownership the RTOS cannot apply priority inheritance; use a mutex so inversion stays bounded.

gotchas.trap: Acquiring locks in inconsistent orders across tasks.
gotchas.correction: That enables circular wait; always acquiring Lock X before Lock Y across all tasks breaks a Coffman condition and prevents deadlock.

gotchas.trap: Calling a standard blocking RTOS API from an ISR.
gotchas.correction: Use FromISR variants (e.g. xQueueSendFromISR / xSemaphoreGiveFromISR); ISRs must only clear the flag and wake a task.
Stack overflow often silently overwrites adjacent task memory (often the TCB), causing hard-to-debug crashes.
